newsitem.title: PERU: Chronology of Peru's 3-week-old hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Chronology of Peru's 3-week-old hostage crisis.

text.p: Marxist rebels of Peru's Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) stunned the world on Dec. 17 when they stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima and took about 500 hostages.
Here is a chronology of the main events so far in the crisis, which entered its 21st day on Tuesday.

TUESDAY, Dec. 17 - About 20 heavily armed guerrillas blow a hole in the wall at Japanese ambassador's Morihisa Aoki's home at 8 p.m. EST (0100 GMT) and swarm in to capture around 500 people, including government officials and foreign diplomats, attending a cocktail party. The rebels release about 80 women and elderly people in the hours soon after the attack.
WEDNESDAY, Dec. 18 - The guerrillas threaten to kill their hostages unless the government frees up to 500 jailed comrades.
THURSDAY, Dec. 19 - Four ambassadors are released to set up a "communications channel" between the rebels and the government.
FRIDAY, Dec. 20 - The rebels release 38 hostages and promise to free another "significant" number.

SATURDAY, Dec. 21 - President Alberto Fujimori, in his first public words since the crisis began, says he will not use force and will study a non-violent "way out" if the guerrillas lay down arms and free all hostages.
SUNDAY, Dec. 22 - The guerrillas release 225 hostages not linked to the government as a "Christmas gesture."
TUESDAY, Dec. 24 - Red Cross officials deliver Christmas cake and a Mass is held inside. The rebels release Uruguay's ambassador after his country frees two MRTA prisoners.
WEDNESDAY, Dec. 25 - Japanese diplomat Kenji Hirata is released in a wheelchair due to his delicate health condition.

THURSDAY, Dec. 26 - An explosion is heard at the residence in the early hours, but Red Cross officials later report there are no injuries. Guatemalan ambassador Jose Maria Argueta is freed as an "acknowledgement of the peace process" in his country.

SATURDAY, Dec. 28 - Government negotiator Domingo Palermo enters the residence for the first face-to-face negotiations with the MRTA. The meeting is followed by the release of 20 hostages and a conciliatory rebel statement expressing willingness "to withdraw from the occupied residence by way of dialogue."
MONDAY, Dec. 30 - The Red Cross brokers an agreement between the government and rebels that will allow the media to approach the besieged residence and film it close-up.

TUESDAY, Dec. 31 - At the invitation of the rebels, the cameramen enter the building and interview guerrilla leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini. The rebels accuse Fujimori of being a dictator aloof from Peru's poor and reassert their demand for the release of their jailed comrades.
Later, Honduras' ambassador Juan Eduardo Martell and Argentina's diplomat Juan Ibanez are freed.
WEDNESDAY, Jan. 1 - Rebels release seven more captives -- including a government official and Peruvian and Japanese businessmen -- to bring the hostage total to 74.
THURSDAY, Jan. 2 - Fujimori speaks for the second time on the crsis. He calls the MRTA attack an isolated incident and claims pointless, "terrorist" violence has increased the number of poor in Peru.

SATURDAY, Jan. 4 - The rebels crawl onto the roof in the small hours and unfurl three banners that warn Fujimori "arrogant" speeches will not solve the crisis. They also say will not give up and that the siege will not end without negotiations.
SUNDAY, Jan. 5 - Bolivian Foreign Minister Antonio Aranibar arrives in Lima to try to find a solution to the siege.
MONDAY, Jan. 6 - An end to the the 20-day crisis looks further away than ever as there are no signs of negotiators or mediators at the site.

The remaining hostages include the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, Fujimori's brother, Pedro, top Peruvian government and security force officials, and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
